config.title: Performance, Memory & Event Loop

intro.title: Performance, Memory & Event Loop
intro.body: In this lesson, you will build a simple interactive web page that demonstrates how JavaScript handles tasks efficiently using the event loop. You will learn core concepts like performance optimization, memory management, and asynchronous execution. The main technologies involved are JavaScript functions, timers, and event listeners. By the end, you'll understand how to write code that avoids blocking the main thread and manages resources effectively.
intro.usecase: Understanding performance, memory, and the event loop is critical for building smooth, responsive applications like interactive dashboards or real-time data feeds. For example, in a financial dashboard updating live stock charts, efficient memory management prevents leaks that slow the app, while the event loop ensures UI updates (like rendering new data points) don't block user interactions (like filtering or sorting). Developers use these concepts to optimize tasks such as debouncing search inputs in large datasets or implementing virtual scrolling in long lists, ensuring the product remains fast and stable under heavy use.

objectives: Implement a function that demonstrates the blocking nature of synchronous code on the event loop.
Construct a memory-efficient data structure to store and manipulate a large dataset.
Apply performance measurement techniques using the Performance API to time code execution.
Configure a setTimeout callback to illustrate asynchronous execution and the callback queue.
Manipulate the order of operations by controlling the microtask queue with Promise.resolve.
Initialize a web worker to offload intensive computations and prevent main thread blocking.
Integrate a debounce function to optimize event handler performance for frequent user inputs.

steps.title: Import console and performance APIs
steps.instruction: In JavaScript, you can directly use browser APIs like console and performance without import statements. Write a simple function named measurePerformance that logs a message to the console using console.log and accesses the performance.now() method.
steps.hint: Create a function that logs a message and calls performance.now(). No imports are needed in plain JavaScript.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named measurePerformance is created that uses console.log and performance.now() to log performance data.
successCriteria: The function measurePerformance is defined, uses console.log, and calls performance.now() without any import statements.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function is named measurePerformance and includes both console.log and performance.now().
steps.feedbackWrong: Check your function name and syntax. Remember, you don't need import statements for console and performance in plain JavaScript.

steps.title: Initialize variables to demonstrate memory allocation
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, create four variables: a string, a number, an array, and an object.
steps.hint: Declare variables using const or let, assigning each a value of the appropriate type.
steps.expectedOutcome: The main function will contain four variables representing different JavaScript data types.

steps.title: Create memory leak example with detached DOM references
steps.instruction: Inside the main function, create a function named createDetachedReferences that creates a DOM element and stores it in a global variable to simulate a memory leak.
steps.hint: Define a function that creates a div element using document.createElement and assigns it to a variable declared outside the function scope.
steps.expectedOutcome: You will have a function that demonstrates how keeping references to DOM elements outside their intended scope can cause memory leaks.
successCriteria: The createDetachedReferences function exists inside main, creates a DOM element, and assigns it to a variable that persists beyond the function's scope.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function creates a DOM element and stores it in a way that prevents garbage collection (like assigning to a global variable).
steps.feedbackWrong: The function doesn't properly demonstrate a memory leak. It should create a DOM element and keep a reference to it that persists beyond the function's execution.

steps.title: Create performance measurement function
steps.instruction: Create a function named measurePerformance that takes a callback function as a parameter and uses performance.now() to measure how long it takes to execute that callback.
steps.hint: Inside the function, record a start time, execute the callback, record an end time, then calculate and return the difference.
steps.expectedOutcome: You'll have a measurePerformance function that can be used to time any callback function's execution.
successCriteria: The measurePerformance function is defined, takes a callback parameter, uses performance.now() to measure execution time, and returns the duration.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure your function takes a callback parameter, calls performance.now() before and after executing it, and returns the time difference.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function isn't quite right. Review the example: you need to capture start/end times with performance.now() and calculate the difference after executing the callback.

steps.title: Create synchronous blocking function
steps.instruction: Inside your main function, create a function named simulateBlocking that performs a heavy synchronous computation (like a large loop) to demonstrate blocking behavior.
steps.hint: Define a function that uses a for loop to iterate many times, performing a simple operation inside the loop.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named simulateBlocking is defined inside main, ready to demonstrate synchronous blocking behavior.
successCriteria: The simulateBlocking function is defined with a loop that performs many iterations.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've defined a function, but it might not perform enough computation to clearly demonstrate blocking. Ensure it has a loop with many iterations.
steps.feedbackWrong: The simulateBlocking function is not defined correctly. Make sure to create a function inside main that performs heavy synchronous computation.

steps.title: Create asynchronous non-blocking function
steps.instruction: Inside the main function, create a new function named simulateNonBlocking that uses setTimeout to demonstrate non-blocking asynchronous behavior.
steps.hint: Use setTimeout to schedule a callback that logs a message after a delay, showing how async code allows other operations to continue.
steps.expectedOutcome: A simulateNonBlocking function is added to main that uses setTimeout to demonstrate non-blocking behavior.
successCriteria: The simulateNonBlocking function is defined inside main and uses setTimeout with a callback.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure your function uses setTimeout and is properly defined inside the main function.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function wasn't created correctly. Remember to define simulateNonBlocking inside main and use setTimeout with a callback function.

steps.hint: Define a function that returns a Promise and logs messages to demonstrate microtask execution order.
steps.expectedOutcome: A demonstrateMicrotask function is added to main that returns a Promise and logs messages about microtasks.
successCriteria: The demonstrateMicrotask function is defined inside main and returns a Promise.

successCriteria: console.log statements are added inside main() before each function call to log execution order.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some console.log statements, but make sure to add them before each function call inside main() to properly track execution order.
steps.feedbackWrong: The console.log statements aren't properly placed inside main() to track execution order. Add console.log('...') before each function call to show when they execute.
